entity_title: Get the DOLE work permit before the work visa
fact_text: A foreign national hired in the Philippines needs an Alien Employment Permit (AEP) from the Department of Labor and Employment before the Bureau of Immigration will issue the 9(g) work visa. The BI's own 9(g) checklist lists the AEP, plus proof the job vacancy was published in a newspaper, as required documents. The AEP is a separate DOLE process, not part of the visa.
evidence_quote: Photocopy of Alien Employment Permit (AEP) issued by the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE);

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the 9(g) work visa is the only approval needed to work. Actually DOLE's AEP is a separate prerequisite the Bureau of Immigration requires before granting the visa. Action: file the AEP with DOLE and complete the job-vacancy newspaper publication first, then lodge the 9(g).

entity_title: Don't work on a tourist visa while the 9(g) is pending
fact_text: While a 9(g) work-visa application is being processed, a foreign national may not lawfully work on a tourist visa. The Bureau of Immigration issues a Provisional Work Permit (PWP) so the person can begin working during the pendency of the pre-arranged employment visa application.
evidence_quote: Issued to a foreign national during the pendency of an application for pre-arranged employment visa.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can start working as soon as you arrive, or the moment the 9(g) is filed. Actually you need a Provisional Work Permit to work legally while the 9(g) is still pending. Action: apply for the PWP at the BI Main Office so the employee can start without working illegally.

entity_title: The 9(g) work visa is employer-petitioned, not self-applied
fact_text: The 9(g) pre-arranged employment visa is the standard long-term work visa for a foreign professional employed by a Philippine company. It covers a foreign national proceeding to the Philippines to engage in a lawful occupation for wages or salary, and is applied for through the hiring company as petitioner.
evidence_quote: Foreign nationals who are proceeding to Philippines to engage in any lawful occupation, whether for wages or salary or other forms of compensation

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a professional can obtain a Philippine work visa on their own. Actually the 9(g) is petitioned by the hiring Philippine company; there is no self-sponsored work visa. Action: have the employer file the petition, since the individual cannot lodge it alone.

entity_title: Visa-free entry is only 30 days, and it is not a work permit
fact_text: Most nationalities are admitted to the Philippines as tourists for an initial stay of only 30 days, extendable first by a 29-day visa waiver. Tourist status does not authorise employment, so a professional cannot legally work under it while employment paperwork is arranged.
evidence_quote: Foreign nationals who are admitted with an initial stay of thirty (30) days may apply for a visa waiver first, granting an additional stay of twenty nine (29) in the Philippines.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed visa-free entry lasts a couple of months. Actually the initial admission is 30 days (then a 29-day waiver) and confers no right to work. Action: plan the AEP/9(g) timeline against the 30-day clock and extend the tourist stay legally in the meantime.

entity_title: Tourist extensions are capped — you cannot stay indefinitely on them
fact_text: A tourist cannot extend forever. Under BI rules a visa-required national may extend a tourist stay up to 24 months and a non-visa-required national up to 36 months, counted from the latest recorded arrival. Beyond that limit the person must hold a proper visa such as the 9(g).
evidence_quote: Under Immigration Memorandum Circular No. SBM-2013-003, non-visa required national may extend their stay up to thirty six (36) months while visa required national may extend their stay up to twenty four (24) months.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can keep extending a tourist visa as long as you keep paying. Actually there is a hard cap (24 months visa-required / 36 months non-visa-required) from your latest arrival. Action: convert to a work or resident visa well before the cap is reached.

entity_title: You must carry an ACR I-Card once your stay passes 59 days
fact_text: Any foreign national whose stay in the Philippines exceeds 59 days must register for and hold an ACR I-Card, a microchip-based, credit-card-sized ID issued by the Bureau of Immigration. It is the government-issued foreigner ID relied on for banking, health insurance and exit clearance.
evidence_quote: An ACR I-Card is a microchip based, credit card-sized, identification card issued to all registered aliens whose stay in the Philippines has exceeded fifty-nine (59) days.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a passport and visa are sufficient ID. Actually anyone staying beyond 59 days must obtain the ACR I-Card, which is needed to open a bank account, register with PhilHealth and leave the country. Action: budget time and fees for the ACR I-Card during onboarding.

entity_title: The ACR I-Card is applied for together with your visa
fact_text: The ACR I-Card is not a separate later errand. The Bureau of Immigration requires the ACR I-Card application to be submitted together with the visa application, and for a 9(g) applicant the fingerprint and photo capture for the card is done as part of the visa process.
evidence_quote: ACR I-Card application must be submitted together with the application for visa.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the ID card is arranged separately after the visa is granted. Actually the ACR I-Card application is filed together with the visa application. Action: prepare ACR I-Card documents and fees at the same time as the 9(g) petition.

entity_title: Long-stay visa holders need an exit clearance even for a short trip
fact_text: A foreign national holding an immigrant or non-immigrant visa (such as the 9(g)) with a valid ACR I-Card must obtain an Emigration Clearance Certificate (ECC-B) before leaving the Philippines, even for a temporary trip abroad. Without it, departure can be stopped at the airport.
evidence_quote: ECC-B is issued to departing holders of Immigrant and Non-Immigrant visas with valid ACR I-Cards and are leaving the country temporarily.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a valid visa and ACR I-Card are all you need to fly out. Actually 9(g) and other immigrant/non-immigrant visa holders need an ECC-B even for a temporary departure. Action: secure the ECC-B before any international trip.

entity_title: Apply for the ECC at least 72 hours before your flight
fact_text: The Bureau of Immigration allows a foreign national to apply for the Emigration Clearance Certificate at least 72 hours before departure. Leaving it to the day of the flight risks being unable to board, because the clearance must be processed in advance.
evidence_quote: A foreign national may apply for an ECC at least 72 hours prior to his/her departure from the Philippines.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the ECC can be sorted at the airport on the day of travel. Actually it should be applied for at least 72 hours before departure. Action: file the ECC three or more days ahead of any trip.

entity_title: An ECC is valid one month and works only once
fact_text: An Emigration Clearance Certificate is valid for one month from issue but may be used only once, regardless of the remaining validity. A new ECC is required for each departure, so one cannot be reused across multiple trips.
evidence_quote: The ECC is valid for one (1) month from the date of issue, however, you may only use this once regardless of its validity.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a one-month ECC covers any trips taken within that month. Actually it is single-use even inside its validity window. Action: obtain a fresh ECC for every departure.

entity_title: SSS enrolment is compulsory for employees, foreigners included
fact_text: Social Security System (SSS) coverage is compulsory for private-sector employees under 60 years of age. A foreign national employed by a Philippine company is enrolled and contributed for like a local hire under the Social Security Act (RA 11199); it is a payroll deduction, not optional.
evidence_quote: Employees (EE) from the private sector, including Kasambahay or house helpers, who are not over sixty (60) years of age;

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed SSS is only for Filipino workers. Actually coverage is compulsory for private-sector employees under 60, and foreign employees of a Philippine company are covered too. Action: ensure the employer registers the hire and remits SSS contributions from day one.

entity_title: Foreign workers register for PhilHealth using their ACR I-Card
fact_text: PhilHealth, the national health insurance program, is open to foreign nationals residing or working in the Philippines. Those holding a valid ACR I-Card register by submitting the PhilHealth Member Registration Form for Foreign Nationals at the nearest Local Health Insurance Office.
evidence_quote: Citizens of other countries residing or working in the Philippines with a valid Alien Certificate of Registration Identity Card (ACR I-Card) issued by the Bureau of Immigration may submit their PMRF for Foreign Nationals to the nearest Local Health Insurance Office (LHIO).

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed PhilHealth is for Filipino citizens only. Actually foreign nationals working or residing in the Philippines with an ACR I-Card can register for PhilHealth. Action: use the ACR I-Card and the foreign-national PMRF to enrol at an LHIO.
